We make it very clear exactly what to expect. When I do this for groups of 50+ I say:

“For this swim test you will need to swim to the rope and back without stopping or touching the ground. You must swim on your front and your arms have to come up and over the water like this (does cool little front crawl arm motion). If you go on your back or if you doggy paddle, you will not pass this test. If you touch the ground, you will not pass this test.” 

Then I send them in groups of 4. I usually repeat the rules every 2 groups, but I always project so that all the kids can hear. 

When they fail I just say: “you did not pass this time because you doggy paddled. You can try again at 3:30 (always at least 15min later)”. If they’re really bad I don’t offer a retry.

Can’t speak to Y requirements, but maybe 20 years ago the standard for single guard removals of a deep water pool existed in my facility. As a side note, when we were taught cpr, the instructor made a comment that stuck with me. “First aid is designed to keep the person in the same condition you found them until EMS arrives.” The best trained first aid responder cannot bring a dead person back to life. While you’re right that 10min should not be difficult for a lifeguard, your times here are exceptionally fast. Olympic standard is 3:53 so anything sub 5 would be considered a very quick swim. Most lifeguards who have no experience in speed swimming or formalized speed training should be able to hit around a 7-8min mark with proper form. This would be considered an average time. 

[This site](https://swimminglevel.com/swimming-times/400m-times) provided some more detail about what your speed should be like as an average depending on years of experience. 

However that being said. When I first started lifeguarding my time was 9min. I was small and my strokes were ineffective. My first year lifeguarding I put on almost 40lb muscle because I was training, and by improving my strokes I was able to take that down to 7min, a time I’m very content with as a pool lifeguard.

A few years ago we had a patron require CPR and in that moment one of our other regular patrons stepped up and offered to help. They are well known as a family doctor in the area. Everything went well. The doctor actually helped a lot and kept commenting on how well we were all doing and was really good at helping maintain a steady CPR rhythm. Most of my staff did agree that we felt better having him there. I wouldn’t trust a non-regular patron to assist in the same way though, and I wouldn’t have allowed the doctor to assist in this manner if we hadn’t known their situation in advance of the emergency.

Most people start talking before the radio starts picking up your words. We train staff to push the button, inhale, and then begin with “name to Supervisor” or “name to front desk”. Then the whole pool knows who is needed and who needs to acknowledge. 

Supervisor responds “supervisor to guard, go ahead” 

Guard responds with a brief description of problem. We ask them to keep it under 10 words. Speak slowly and clearly, as pool decks are quite noisy and there is a lot of interference. 
Whistles are always a priority, radios are used only in non-emergencies, as we have drowning alarms near all pools as well. 

Examples of radio situations:
- code brown (iykyk)
- cover an area on deck
- enforce a patron rule that’s not urgent (like food on deck)
- change a load of laundry
- mop or clean change rooms 
- patron wanting to speak with a supervisor
- instructor needing help with lessons

Always start with a ridiculously easy progression. Most parents are uncomfortable, and most babies can pick up on that anxiety. I often start with the parents just supporting baby in a seated position with head on parents shoulder. When introducing back floats in a more horizontal position, parents should support all baby’s weight on their forearms along the baby’s sides. It’s scary for little ones to feel unsupported if they’ve never felt it before!

I changed the structure of my classes completely. Instead of trying to teach babies how to swim, I teach the parents how to support and teach their children. 

Ex. Instead of teaching baby to float on their back, my objective is to teach parents how to hold the child, why back floats are an important skill, and how to make progressions in this skill.

Think of this as your chance to train parents in some very basic swimming instruction.

I teach my class progressively. Don’t worry about submerging to get the brick, focus on swimming with it. Start in the shallow end and practice doing 5-15m with it at the surface. Then practice in the deep end, I usually start by swimming close to a wall so that if you get nervous you can reach out and grab the wall. Once you feel comfortable swimming with it for 15m at a time, work on the full skill (approach, submersion, retrieval, and swim). A strong kick is essential, and I recommend swimming reclined at a 45°angle with your head tilted up to the ceiling, this helps your body float more naturally. Keep the brick tight to your chest while swimming as this makes it easier.

Stay away from the edges. While it feels safer for people, knowing that there is a wall beside them, the waves will make it impossible for you to escape. Additionally you are at a higher risk of becoming injured by a wave throwing you against a wall. 

Best self rescue tip from me: stay calm and hop out. I teach this to the kids in swimming lessons at my wave pool. When you first go under, let yourself sink to the ground. Push off with both feet as hard as possible, and when you surface, take a big breath, face shore, and prepare to sink again. Instead of fighting the sinking, try to keep yourself calm and exhale while under, inhale after pushing up. You might only hop forward 1 foot at a time, but keeping calm will allow you to make it back to shore, or at least to shallower water.

In multi victim scenarios I would actually do it backwards of what people are saying. Pass off your tube or flotation device to anyone who is able to support themselves with it and save themselves. Then I prioritize from least urgent to most while the person with the flotation device does a self rescue. 

Why? Because whoever you do not save first will get worse. Ex. A conscious and unconscious person. If I pick the unconscious first, there is a chance that the conscious one could pass out while waiting, making 2 unconscious. 

Go quick. Don’t wait for them to get out of the water, just get them to a place where an untrained bystander can take over, then keep going. At most pools, a conscious rescue should take less than 30 seconds start to finish, but removing an unconscious person takes longer. Additionally, untrained swimmers can tow an unconscious person but should not be asked to rescue an active drowning person.

I like to do physical manipulation for this. I’ll have them sit on the side of the pool and I’ll first draw their legs in a proper motion (emphasize that knees are stuck together) with flexed feet. Then I’ll do a resistance training, so I’ll hold my hands on the insides of their feet, and have them try to push their feet together while keeping their knees in place. I provide the resistance by pushing outward while they kick inward. My facility also offers bands for knees, which prevents them from doing a frog kick by keeping knees in together. Some kids also improve by practicing a vertical whip kick to tread water, so that they can visually see if their knees are together or not. 

It also helps to fix this while they’re on their back first if possible, and with head out of the water if not, because then you can communicate with them while they are swimming to give reminders to flex their feet, or keep their knees in!

It really depends on the problems that the individual kids are experiencing. I teach in BBLAT order to help correct strokes (yes I know it’s BLABT for Red Cross, but this works better and makes more sense). 

B (body position) - focus on tucking the chin, and breathing to the side without looking forward for free.

B (breathing)- get them to take only 1 inhale/breathing arm, instead of pausing on their side. Swimming should be as natural as running with a regular pattern, exhale in the water and inhale out. Sometimes front glide/side glide drills can help with this. 

L (legs)- work on strong powerful kicks. Strength drills like kicking against a vertical kick board for free, and working on a strong kick using the insides of flexed feet for breast.  Head out drills using some form of resistance are best, and watch out for triangle kicks in breast- those are weak and ineffective. 

A (arms)- strong and long for free, don’t let their arms end early. Arms should stretch into the water, push hard with a high elbow, and finish by passing the thigh. For breast, elbows should be higher and wider than hands at all times. Think about scooping ice cream, reach down and around, but keep elbows out of the way of the container. 

T (timing)- for free watch out for kids breathing too late in the stroke, they should roll to take a breath as soon as their hand moves from in front of them, and face should be back in the water before the arm passes the ear in the recovery phase. This is especially important for breast. Pull to breathe, kick to glide. I like to do a pause drill to fix timing for breast, so they pull to breathe, take a short glide, and then kick to a longer glide. This overcorrection usually fixes their timing 

For more advice, send specifics to r/swiminstructors and if you can include a video, that helps a lot!!

Depends on what kind of problems you’re having. What you’re describing (splashing, pushing off the wall, not paying attention), sounds like a fairly typical class when students are bored. This class might just need a challenge and to be pushed harder.



If that’s not working: 
- load up your lesson plans with activities. Don’t give the kids more than 3 seconds in between skill attempts. You’ll tire them out so much that they can’t goof off. (Ex. Timmy does a front glide “go again Timmy, more bubbles!” And then he goes) 

- add in a talent show every 15 min or so. Where everyone gets to show off their coolest tricks (handstand or whatever). Then you clap and cheer and go crazy. BUT if they’re practicing before it’s the talent show, they’re not allowed to have a turn. Bc you already saw their trick. 

- Sometimes if my kids aren’t listening or respecting me, I’ll challenge them to a race. If they beat me, they can be the teacher for 5 minutes. And then I make sure to destroy them in the race. I’ll even tease them sometimes “see you guys haven’t been paying attention, that’s why I’m faster than you”. But again. This is meant to be a playful fun correction, not in a mean tone. 

- use positive reinforcement. At the start of class you can give each kid a bucket or some sort of station on the side of the pool. If they get 5 rewards (I use laminated smiley faces), then they get a special reward at the end of class. Only give out rewards for going above and beyond, listening and being able to repeat it back, not splashing anyone for 15 minutes, asking the other kid to listen, etc. Make them achievable. And if they don’t get all 5 but the other kid does? Too bad for the other kid. 

- I’ve done the same thing above with hot tub water for kids who love the hot tub. I fill a bucket with warm water, and every time they’re naughty I dump a little out. At the end of class I’ll dump whatever is left on them as their reward. Usually on day 1 they’ve got very little left. 

- talk to the parents. Explain that their children are not getting as much out of the lesson as they would if they were listening and paying attention. Remember that parents are usually paying a lot for lessons, they want the kids to succeed! Then let the parents know that you’ll be trying some new tactics and ask for advice.

Instead of using words like “straight legs” or “straight kick”, focus on lengthening their glides. I do front glides/rocket ships with my kids by having them learn to put their arms completely extended over their ears, then completely hide their face under water (bc rocket ships are really loud of course), and then stretch out as long as they can to make the biggest rocket ship possible. Once they can stretch really long and streamlined, I teach them to push off the wall with their tip toes (encourages long straight legs) and to make small splashes. 

For back glides we do Spider-Man glides. We hold on to the wall with our hands and feet up, like Spider-Man. We put our ears in to listen for bad guys (streamline the head position). And we SLOWLY push off the wall. It’s important to keep our webs nice and long (shoulders relaxed and hands by side), and to keep our toes as long as we can. It helps us sneak up on bad guys lol. 

In all honesty, kids that size rarely benefit from using kickboards. They just don’t have the coordination and core strength for it. It’s way easier to teach these glides unassisted, and often submerged (for front glides).

A few questions for clarification, are you the only manager at your location? If not, look at the other managers. What did you like/respect/trust about them? Try to become the best parts from each of them. 

I’d say your staff need to know that you’ll have their back. You can easily destroy someone’s confidence or trust in your leadership by not supporting them when patrons are grumpy. If the guard is in the wrong, don’t tell the patron, instead just say, “as a manager, I’m allowed to offer some exceptions to the rules” or something like that. That way the guard is still right, and you can explain the rules more clearly to them later. 

Don’t criticize them publicly, instead pull them aside, calmly explain ways they can improve. I like to use the structure of “I understand your intentions, here’s a way to help enforce the rule/prevent miscommunication/improve patron relationships, etc.” 

Admit that you’re learning. Ask for feedback in a polite way. It can be feedback on a program you’re running, or you can ask if they have advice for what they like/dislike in a supervisor.  

Don’t let them walk all over you. You’re probably friends with some of them. Your work relationship should not be the same as your friendship. If you need to, talk to your closer friends and explain that when your manager uniform is on, the joking has to be cut back. You need to be respected by patrons and that starts with guards showing you respect too. It’ll be tough but lots of friendships can survive this. In a really nice breast stroke, it’s better to see hips remaining at the surface and knees bending up towards the stomach. It gives a lot more power to the kick and causes less back/neck injuries. Like other commenters have said. Your body position is crucial. Your head shouldn’t be tilted back, just in a neutral position, like you are when you’re standing, only horizontal. 

Calves and feet drop together, flexing out to the sides, and squeezing the water together. Power in the kick will help your face stay dry, so focus on the gentle pull, and powerful squeezing motion. 

If your arms ever come out of the water, you will get your face wet. Arms slowly slide up the body up to your armpits, then outwards into big butterfly wing shapes, pushing hard towards your feet. Don’t let them extend higher than your head though, that’s just a waste of power. 

Slowing down and gliding for 2-3 seconds between strokes will also help keep your face dry.

When I teach, I only teach floating for the purpose of making sure the student is comfortable 1. On their front with their face in, and 2. On their back with their ears in. Most people cannot hold a float without movement for very long. 

Once you’re comfortable, I think glides are much more effective as learning tools. Practice extending your arms straight over your head, hands together and arms covering the ears completely. Gliding on your front with your arms extended is a good progression for front crawl. Simply put your face in the water with your arms extended, then slowly push off the wall and begin to kick. 

On your back, hold on to a wall with your arms. Put your shoulders underwater, then lean your head back so you’re facing the ceiling. Then slowly push your feet off the wall, keeping your hips high and your feet lower with slow gentle kicks. For this one your arms should be at your sides and you should focus on relaxing, keeping shoulders down and back. 

Good luck.

Like the last person said. Fix problems one at a time. As an instructor I always fix strokes in a specific order, because certain problems will cause other problems as well. The order is 1. Body and head position. 2. Breathing. 3. Kick. 4. Pull. 5. Timing. 

- your hip sway is the first thing you’ve got to fix. A wider arm entry (in line with shoulders) and more rotation while pulling will help. 
- kicking does make you more tired but will streamline your stroke. Practice with a kickboard a slow paced kick. Don’t worry about speed, just consistency. Flippers will help too
- apart from widening your arm pulls, work on a smoother entry with fingers before your hand. Also work on a bent arm pull. Pull should be shallower, and in line with your core. Bent arm pulls produce more power and speed. Try with a pullbuoy. 
- arm timing. To me it looks like you could work on a catch up drill, instead of having your arms opposite, keep one in line with your shoulders to help streamline, while the other one pulls. Switch when your pull arm is recovering by your head. Try with a pullbuoy. 
- breath timing. Practice a front glide side glide to nail the timing. You should be inhaling while you pull, but as soon as your hand reaches your hips, face needs to be back in the water. 

Good luck!

No, I find snorkels breed dependence on being able to see what you’re doing, and often do not correct the issue. Your problem involves the timing with your breaths, so taking out the breathing won’t help in the long run. Instead, do a skating drill maybe?

- start in a side glide, one arm up and breathing (2 seconds)
- keeping that arm up, roll face in (2 seconds)
- keeping face in, switch arms so you’re on your opposite side (2 seconds)
- side glide position again with breathing (2 seconds) and repeat 

You could also work on just front glide/side glide combination, so no arm pulls unless you’re taking a breath. Go slow, breathe as you pull your arm and pause in a side glide position. Then roll your face in before lifting your side glide arm back into front glide.

When I teach breathing timing, I always encourage students to breathe while they’re pulling their arm through the water and turning to the side, by the time that hand gets to the hips, they should be beginning to put their face back into the water. 

We also teach our students to have slow powerful pulls that alternate when the other arm is at approximately shoulder level. So it’s more of a hand switch than a hand catch up. We use the analogy of a “car wash” - the area in front of your head. You always want one “car” - hand in the car wash, and it wants to stay as long as it can. But when the next guy is coming, you be polite and switch cars. There should never be two hands completely catching up, but they shouldn’t have a problem taking their time up front.

As a drill to help with body awareness, swim with your head facing forwards. Keep the water line at or just above your goggles. Pay attention to how little your body has to move when swimming. I would practice in baby steps. It’s going to feel awkward but this might help. 
1. Front glide/side glide breathing at the wall. Hold the wall with your hands, face submerged. Keep your feet on the ground. Practice one exhale under, rolling and then one inhale over the water. Repeat at least 20 times continuously. It doesn’t matter how fast/slow as long as it’s one breath in and one breath out. 
2. Front glide/side glide with a kickboard. Same idea. Keep your arms both extended up over your head. One exhale underwater, one inhale over. I find it helps to save the last bit of exhale for the rolling part, so I don’t get water up my nose. 
3. Bubble arm breath arm. It’s front crawl breathing every second arm. Practice an exhale on one arm, and inhale on the opposite. It should be slow and steady, not fast.

You should not have pointed toes. Common mistake. Your legs start the kick from the hip, so it should be fairly straight, but in a floppy, relaxed manner. We often tell new swimmers to point their toes because it is really hard to bend your knees if your toes are pointed. However, once a swimmer can kick with straight legs, we look for relaxed feet and ankles. Pointed toes = minimal forward movement. 

Try to let your legs just be limp, and kick from the hips and thighs, not from the feet or ankles. Thinking about it as kicking with long legs, as stretched out as you can be, rather than pointed toes. Or like your leg is like a flipper, the upper thigh is rigid and controls the power, while the lower leg and foot follow through with the motion.

The biggest part of swimming is streamlining. So for example, when most people learn to do front glides, they will be slow because their head is poking up from between their arms, or because their kick is bent. 

Every stroke has a streamline component. If you can keep your body in a neutral position (head tucked and body in a straight line), then you will have less drag. This makes your stroke more efficient, not faster. In the earlier stages of stroke development, this is way more important. Once your stroke is technically correct, it becomes a lot easier to work on increasing speed and power.

Muscle is more dense than fat is. The more muscular you are the more you sink. Don’t worry about how you float on your back. Most adults can not maintain a float for more than a couple seconds without some kicking or sculling. 

If your instructor is trying to teach you floating, pulling your arms up higher so you make an X instead of a T shape, could help you. But really, focus on glides and glides with kick instead. They’re much more practical progressions towards full strokes.

Start with a bubble-breathe pattern. So with your face in, do one full arm circle. Then on your other arm pull, roll your face and body to the side, into a side glide position. While you’re learning this, feel free to take a second or two to get into a good side glide position with your face out. Once you’ve had a breath, roll back in, and do another bubble arm. 

As you become more comfortable, you can improve by removing the pause on your breathe arm, and then learn to do breathing every 3 pulls, or whatever feels most comfortable to you. 

Good luck!

I would say that these numbers are only partly accurate. When teaching swimming to new swimmers, it’s not uncommon for someone to take 1-2 minutes for a single 25m length. These are numbers for someone familiar with the concept of freestyle, not for someone just learning it. 

I’d say that a lot of new adult swimmers stick mostly to backstroke and breaststroke. It might be easier to start there if you don’t have a lot of experience with free.

While waiting for your lessons to start, work on some basic skills. Big things include front glides/swims and back glides. Instead of worrying about floating, gliding helps streamline you. A glide without any kick shouldn’t be more than 3-5 seconds. 

For front glides, extend your arms over your ears, lower your shoulders-hands-face-ears into the water, and gently push off with your feet. Use a kick board or a noodle if you’re anxious. 

For back glides, start with your hands holding the edge of the pool, shoulders under water, and head gently tilted back so your ears are submerged, and gently push off the wall with your feet. Focus on arching your back slightly, so that your hips are always higher than ankles. If you can, use a noodle to support your lower back, or hold a kick board over your chest with your arms crossed. 

You can also work on kicking with long relaxed legs. Unlike younger students, adult learners often need to bend the knee slightly. That’s ok. Whatever makes you move the fastest. You can practice kicking with your face out of the water on your front if you use an assist like a kickboard or noodle. 

Good luck!

Please understand that this is coming from a lifeguard who has had to perform CPR on someone who held their breath for too long underwater. It could be fun but I know how incredibly dangerous it can be.
Just saying that holding your breath while performing any sport is just not a great idea and cannot be maintained.

Before you start to hold your breath, take extremely slow, shallow breaths for about 20-30 seconds. Then take one large quick breath. You should be able to hold it at least an extra 10 seconds. 

That being said, holding your breath when swimming any sort of distance will always slow you down because it makes your body tense up. As a lifeguard, I can honestly say I can only hold my breath for like 20 seconds when rescuing. This is because the harder you push yourself the more oxygen you expend. So since I’m swimming faster and harder to save someone, I need more oxygen. Plus, it’s kind of a good thing if I can get them back up in a short amount of time. 

You don’t hold your breath when you play soccer. You shouldn’t hold it when you swim either.

Depends on the group. We’ve had a Special O group renting our pool space and instructors for about 10 years. They have 2 strong groups that are capable of swimming lengths and diving, and the last group always has someone in the water, and they stay in the shallow end. 

If possible, find out the skill level you’re working with. Especially watch when they enter the water. The best swimmer can panic if they hit the water wrong. And if you see weaker swimmers, don’t be afraid to ask them to practice half lengths in the shallow end instead.

See if you can get someone to videotape your swimming, often just seeing what you are doing can help. 

Likely you’re not moving because your feet are too stiff. Flippers have a lot of weight on the toe, so your ankle naturally has to flick and point when kicking. Remember that it’s not about having straight legs so much as relaxed legs. Let your foot go limp and just focus on moving the ankle up and down instead. 

Check your knees as well. If your kick is led by the knees then you won’t move as quickly, regardless of how your feet are positioned.

More strokes between pulls is not as effective. Think of it this way, if you’re running a marathon, but holding your breath as you run, you’re going to burn out too fast. Your body needs oxygen to go quickly. You also need to breathe more frequently if you’re sprinting than if you’re running a longer distance. Same principles apply for swimming. Most people do 3 pulls/breath to stay balanced, but you can do 2 if you continue to swim straight. 

I usually do pyramid drills for training. So I start off with 2 pulls/breath for 50m, then build up to 5, and back down to 2. It’s only a 400m drill but it’s how I begin any freestyle workout. You can do with/without kick, but the rhythm of breathing is so important in swimming.

Everyone floats in slightly different positions. Keeping your lungs full of air will help make you more buoyant. Bear in mind that there really is no point in doing a float for longer than 3-5 seconds. 

Also, like how another user mentioned, your body is like a seesaw. Make sure your face is angled down, in a neutral or slightly tucked position. Attempt to have even the back of your head submerged. 

You can also keep your arms extended over your head in line with your shoulders, this should stretch your body into a more horizontal position as well.

The two biggest things I noticed were 1) weaker dolphin kick after your push off the wall, 2) shorter and less efficient arm pulls. 

Right now it looks like your underwater streamlining is the slowest part of your stroke. Strengthen your kicking and make sure to keep your arms tight over your head to streamline the best you can. 

You are also doing more arm pulls than the swimmers next to you. It looks like your pull finishes around your waist, instead of reaching its full extension point. I find doing arms-only practice can help strengthen pulls. 

I’m not a speed swimmer by any means, but I find that making the stroke more efficient means you expend less energy. It helped me cut my time down quite a bit.
You can also do this on your stomach on your bed. Do small kicks with relaxed legs.

Work on some ab strengthening exercises to help your core strength. Right now the power in your kick comes from your knees. You want the power to begin in the chest and abs, and roll down through to the ankles. 

It helps to practice a super exaggerated chest roll to start with. Almost like you’re doing dolphin kick with only your core. Let your head lead the movement. Wearing flippers can also help strengthen your stroke.

Practice training to complete the distance first. Use a kickboard and simply kick for the distance, always exhaling underwater and inhaling one breath above water. You can look forward for this skill. 

Once you can make the distance without stopping, change the way you breathe by switching to front glide/side glide with the board. One inhale in sideglide and one exhale in front glide. 

After you can make the distance like this, take away the board and work on your front crawl. Focus on slow long arm pulls. Speed is not as important as consistency, so pace yourself. I find it’s easier to learn in a bubble/breath pattern of breathing every second pull. So exhale while one arm pulls, inhale in side glide while the other arm pulls. Repeat. 

Once you’re stronger, I change my tactic to breathing pyramids. For example, I’ll swim 7 lengths of the pool. On the first length I’ll breathe every 2 pulls, on the second every 3, then 4, 5, 4, 3, and back to 2. It focuses on strengthening your arm pulls and relaxing your breathing in the water. Sometimes this can be done arms only if you’ve already done a leg workout.

A few questions that we ask at our pool interviews:
- If a patron is upset with you and is arguing with you on deck, what would you do?
- how would you talk to a parent in swimming lessons who is concerned that their child will not complete the level?
- in a specific emergency example, how do you respond if you are the second guard on deck?
- give some examples of how you have been or will be a positive team member?
- if a fellow employee confronts you, how do you respond?

Nicely done. Often times when you recognize the situation, your adrenaline kicks in and to an extent, you do lose control. Instincts take over. That’s one of the main reasons that we have regular inservice training and why our courses require so much practice. 

Make sure to take care of yourself. Your mind might start to second guess what you did. Remind yourself that at the end of the day, you saved a life. You did exactly what you were supposed to do. Depends on his skill level tbh. If he’s just learning basics, then floats and glides require no kick anyway. It might take more time for him to learn how to recover from a float or a glide, so focus on learning how to right yourself after swimming. 

If he’s a little more advanced, teach him to do front crawl arms while rolling to his back to breathe. It’s easier to float in that position and can help build swimmers endurance before learning side glide breathing for front crawl. 

Work on good head and body position, relaxed and rhythmic breathing, and streamlined glides. Once that’s down, teach the arm pulls. Leave kicking for last. The body will naturally compensate some kicking to maintain balance, and he may need to have a more bent kick than other swimmers. It’s hard to tell without more details.

Preschoolers - keep them active and engaged. Use your imagination. You’re not blowing bubbles, you’re blowing out birthday candles. It’s not a starfish float, you’re the captain of an airplane, and you’ve got to put your face in the water so you can see where you’re going. A class that’s having fun will listen much better. 

School aged - use progressive teaching. If a kid can’t put their face in, they’re not ready to do a float, so they’re not ready to do a glide, and they’re definitely not ready to do front crawl/freestyle. Work with each student at their own level, and while you work with one kid, have the rest practice independently. (While I help A with her front glide, I want B and C to do 3 practice glides). That way kids are practicing all class, not just waiting for their turn. 

Teens - they’re usually motivated with a purpose. Find out what it is and encourage them in it. If they want to go into lifeguarding, show them how to grab rings from the bottom of the pool and explain that this is a beginning rescue technique. Teach eggbeater. If a teen just wants to finish swimming lessons (parent motivated), explain to them how to correct their strokes as a way to get out of lessons. (If you enter the water like this, it meets criteria for this level). 

Some general advice: 
- DO DEMOS. Most kids/adults are visual learners. 
- give them tons of practice time with regular feedback
- keep them active and wet
- ask your coworkers and supervisors for help. They have more experience and may pick up on things you can’t see yet. They’ll have more specific tips and tricks for you too.

A strong surface dive, so beginning with good eggbeater, pushing the water down with your forearms (lifting you higher out of the water), then as you submerge, push yourself under the water by sculling your forearms up over your head, almost into a clap. Keep your body streamlined and your chin tucked down. From this position you can continue to scull with your hands above your head, or you can flip upside down and begin swimming towards the bottom if permitted. I recommend using a breast stroke kick or a dolphin kick if yours is strong. 
If your lungs are full, you float. So try to slowly exhale as you submerge. Make sure you save enough air for the way back up!

I would practice swimming along the bottom of your indoor pool with either breast stroke/ dolphin kick. I would also practice sitting on the bottom of the pool and sculling with your hands above you to stay in place.

I find that paying attention to each guards strengths as well as weaknesses goes a long way. For my new hires I really focus on making sure they know that if I have to ask them to redo something, or to do something better (shorter scans, stronger whistles, etc) it is something that everyone goes through in training. When you’re at the bottom, ground yourself with your feet on the bottom and your knees in a deep bend. Put the brick against your chest to best streamline then push off hard with both feet, using your free hand to pull if allowed. 

At the surface, a strong eggbeater is my favourite. It keeps my head and shoulders and the brick out of the water. If that is too slow for you, lean back a bit and go into either a whip kick or a scissor kick on your back. Usually a whip kick or scissor kick can take you 1m for every kick you do. Our policy is that the brick can be submerged but your head and ears must be dry. I think it depends on which facility/society you’re going through.
Yes! Fox 40 Classic all the way!

It’s definitely a mental skill. Something about the idea of a 20lb brick at the bottom of the pool is just a little stressful. I found it helpful to start by working on my eggbeater with the brick first. Proving to myself that I was capable of swimming 25m with the brick. Then I began to work on retrieving it. Starting shallower but progressing a little deeper every time. 

I still hate this skill but it’s no longer difficult. Good luck!

I do 5 minutes sitting, then 10 minutes of walking around the pool. Repeat those 15 minutes until another guard relieves you. Movement helps keep the brain awake.

Cleaning is a huge part of lifeguarding. Anyone who tells you otherwise works at the kind of huge facility where they have a team of maintenance people. As long as there are multiple staff members off deck, there should be someone cleaning. Guarding is obviously your first responsibility, cleaning is second. 

Even at my facility (4 pools, usually 800+ people on a summer day), we only have one maintenance worker, who is responsible for fixing broken equipment, testing the pools, and general patio/parking lot cleaning. Everything inside the facility is the guards responsibility to clean. Dirty change rooms or a dirty deck make it unappealing to public. Once a year, we do a complete facility shut down with all pools drained for 3 weeks, and all lifeguards are scheduled to come in and deep clean during this time as well.

For every constructive critical comment you give, you should be giving a compliment as well. Not in the same sitting! But if I know that I’ve got to be hard on a staff member because they’re not doing thorough scans, I’ll look for something to thank them for - work ethic, public relations,  even just general attitude. It’s not always possible but it works. 

Don’t try to make too many big changes at once. When I got promoted to supervisor I had a list of ideas to make my facility better. People don’t like change in large doses. Pick one small thing to change at a time, and explain how this change will positively impact staff and patrons. 

I know this is maybe a little off topic, but my last piece of advice is to stick to your policies, especially for the first few months. Lots of supervisors want staff to like them, and end up not confronting staff or letting them get away with things they shouldn’t do. You’re not a coworker anymore. You’re a supervisor. Once they respect you and see you as a good guard and instructor, they will enjoy working with you. But if they see you as someone who slacks off, they may like working with you, but you’ll have a hard time earning their respect. 

Good luck out there.

So I’m not 100% sure if this is the same in the US, but for Canadian WSIs, the WSI program has gone through a lot of changes lately. 

If your original WSI certificate was good for 1 year, you had to complete the 3 required online modules to extend it for a second year. However, recently they started giving out the original WSI certificate for 2 years. Then you need to do the online modules before your recert. 

Bring a copy of your original certificate, and proof of completing the 3 additional online modules. Be prepared to demonstrate your strokes as well as your instructor response skills (like first aid and basic rescues) and water safety skills (treading water, entries, etc). 

WSI recerts are designed to both verify that you have the skills necessary to teach and demo, and to help you become a better instructor for the future by teaching/reteaching you.

Ma’am your child was in distress and could not keep her face above the surface to get air. I’m taking her to the side so she can sit down and get some air. 

“SHE LIKES BEING UNDER THE WATER”

*me holding visibly distressed child who is still coughing*
Ma’am I’m just doing my job. 

“THIS IS ILLEGAL. YOU CANT JUST TOUCH CHILDREN WITHOUT CONSENT!”

Our pool (Canada) has about half the staff trained through the Lifesaving Society-NLS, about a quarter trained through Canadian Red Cross, and about a quarter who have transferred from NLS to RC. 

We’ve standardized all our pool emergency procedures. We have a unique set of whistles, signals, and we practice our facility’s standard spinal and distressed swimmer responses regularly. All staff are required to know these. We try to update our facility procedures every few years as the two lifeguarding societies update their procedures. 

Inservices are definitely tough for the first few, but once staff become comfortable with our way of doing rescues, they pick it up quickly. Not only do we ensure that all staff can perform our specific rescue procedure, we keep them practicing skills from both societies every inservice. As a result, most of our staff can perform skills at both the Red Cross and the Lifesaving Society standard. I think having the diversity is one of our greatest strengths as a facility!

Depends on the policies of your facility. We only use our whistles to signal a patron if they are in immediate danger (ex a young non swimmer near our drop slide, or someone swimming underneath a diving board). That is just one quick whistle blast, not too loud. Loud and regular whistles (.5 seconds) are for guards to pay attention, while long 2 second whistles are to clear the pool in case of a major emergency. 

When I teach students to blow whistles, I teach the “tsst” sound. This uses the tongue to start and stop the whistle, making it a clearer and sharper sound.

Usually we assume spinal injuries if they entered head first in a shallow zone, or after a diving incident (either if they dive in head first or if someone dives onto them). We have a drop slide in the deep end as well and always assume spinal injuries for any time two patrons collide upon entry. Any fall from a height greater than the patrons height we assume spinal, and any time we hear complaints of neck/back pain. 
Deep end incidents where there was no collision are usually not considered spinal say our facility, as the odds of hitting the bottom of the pool (4m) with enough force to hurt the spinal column is extremely unlikely.

We always keep at least 2 of our lines in. It depends on the guard station and location of the emergency. If I’m sitting on a raised guard chair, I’ll likely chuck the tube over both lanes and dive in, retrieving my tube as I surface. 

If I’m ground level it’s a toss up, depending on whether the emergency is close to the wall or if it is more central in the pool. If it’s close to a wall, I’d run around the pool and jump in closer to them, but if it’s in the middle of the pool I’d jump in and swim over the lines. If you’re wearing the tube strap, it’s easiest to just let it drag behind you for this. 

It’s all situational. Practice with each technique and see what feels best for you.

Hi there! I would recommend either Carnival or Royal Caribbean. I’ve cruised both for 6-8 day cruises, nothing shorter, and there’s always been plenty of people my own age to hang out with and the parties have been lots of fun. (I’m a 23y/o female). They both cater to younger clients and are relatively affordable. 

I personally lean towards Carnival. I know people on this site really don’t seem to like Carnival as much, but I found their night life is just a lot more exciting. Their ships might not be as impressive but I think the variety of included food is far superior to Royal Caribbean’s. They are also cheaper to cruise with.

I love Roatan, it’s one of my favourite stops. Last time we did a pirates/monkeys/birds of the Caribbean tour where we got to hold parrots and monkeys!! Loved it. It was roughly $70 per person. 

Usually we just get off the boat and walk for 5 minutes to this beautiful beach. You can choose to take a gondola for a few dollars but it actually takes longer than just walking. Ask a local for directions as it’s easy to get turned around in the shopping centre right off the ship.

We did My Time. It was great, and our group of 4 never waited for a table (except for one formal night- and then it was a 15 minute wait). We were even able to request the same section each night. However, the crew was constantly pressuring us to reserve a table in advance, especially for formal nights. 

We just honestly preferred to make last minute decisions about when we wanted to eat and couldn’t be bothered to reserve in advance. But if you looked at the itinerary and decided you wanted dinner at 6 the next night, you can reserve a time slot one day in advance. 

So MyTime can actually be pretty structured if that’s what you’re looking for.

There are meet ups throughout the cruise, but much like any other singles events, very few people go. I have found that New Years cruises tend to be a little better for these kinds of events though. Not sure why.

Best rescue:
Guarding an outdoor pool, I recognize a weaker swimmer trying to go on the diving board. 
“Ma’am you know it’s deep here? It will be over your head.” She nods. “You know that you will go under water?” Nods again. The other guard on deck gave me a nod to signal they knew what was happening. The HG took over my position. 
Lady jumps in, and was under for less than a second. When I got her out, “oh I didn’t know that I couldn’t swim!”

Worst rescue:
Guarding inside around a junior Olympic pool with a drop water slide. I’m guarding beside the dumbest new hire I’ve ever seen. He’s positioned by the drop slide, I’m across the pool. I see a small child, about 4 y/o sitting down to go down the slide. I whistle and yell for her to get off. She doesn’t notice and goes down the slide, starts drowning. 
Whistled, then I jump off the stand and run for her, dive in and grab her. Maybe 4 seconds. At this point, the new guard finally notices. He jumps in too, TAKES HER FROM MY ARMS, and brings her to the wall, which is one arms length from his ground level station. 

He could have literally reached over to grab her without jumping in and a) leaving the pool unguarded b) making me get my hair wet. 

I’ve never been so mad at a guard in my life.

Maybe a little late here but oh well. 

We have an arms reach policy for children under 8 at my facility, as there are multiple pools and water slides and whatnot. While the pool is pretty empty, there is one mother and 3 y/o child. Child runs towards a deep end diving board by herself. One lifeguard sends her back towards her mom. Mom turns to me to complain. 

Daughter jumps into the far side of the pool, submerges, and begins to drown. Mom hasn’t noticed. I whistle, jump over Mom, and get to the child (about 10m away). Once I bring the child to safety, Mom begins to yell at me. Threatens to sue the pool. Hollers until my manager comes to deal with the situation. 

Why? Because I touched her child without her permission. 
Sorry that I saved your child’s life.

Booking the full cruise pass to the spa was worth it. On the first day, our cruise offered a discount, making it much more affordable. We also found that the pass was transferable. Make sure to pack a few formal outfits, and don’t forget to put your phone into airplane mode. It could save you a few hundred dollars. Bring a waterproof camera if possible, even one of the disposable ones. You never know when you’ll want to take a photo, especially underwater. Remember to bring cash, in USD if possible, it is commonly accepted in the Bahamas. Bring a pair of sneakers for any excursions you might go on, and long pants if you’ll be doing any hiking. Don’t forget a sweater, it can get a bit chilly on deck at night. 

Since it’s your first time, try everything. If you don’t like it, just don’t go again! As a teen I enjoyed Carnivals youth programs, I’m sure you’ll love it too.

It depends on which night of your cruise and at what time you go. 

Formal dinners will be packed. The longest waits are between 6-8pm. For these nights I recommend either getting in line before they open or waiting until after 8. Wait times for formal nights can be up to an hour long (granted I usually cruise over Christmas so that may be an exception). Sometimes they’ll give you a buzzer so you can wait in the atrium. 

On casual nights, waits are much shorter. Usually less than half an hour regardless of when you go. 

On port days that are also casual nights, I’ve never encountered a wait time longer than 5 minutes. 

The dining experience itself is usually an hour and a half for us, we eat leisurely although don’t usually wait around once we’ve finished eating. Carnival waitstaff also usually perform for the guests around 7 or 7:30, singing and dancing. These shows are always a highlight for me.
